title: 基于自适应的机器学习的自然语言处理模型
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to natural language processing (NLP) utilizing an adaptive machine learning model. Traditional NLP models often rely on static parameters, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex contextual scenarios. We introduce a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism within the model, allowing it to adapt to the nuances of the input text and improve both language understanding and generation capabilities. This design facilitates more robust and accurate performance across a wider range of linguistic tasks. The proposed model leverages a combination of techniques, including contextualized word embeddings, a differentiable parameter update strategy, and a feedback loop to refine model parameters based on the input text's context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through empirical evaluation on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in language understanding and generation tasks.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Topological Network Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed learning leveraging the dynamic topology of quantum entanglement networks. The core idea is to exploit entanglement-based quantum routing to facilitate direct information exchange between nodes, bypassing the limitations of classical communication bottlenecks. Furthermore, the evolving topology of the network is utilized to optimize the learning process. We introduce a mathematical framework to describe this system, focusing on the key concepts of entanglement distribution, quantum routing, and topological network evolution. The proposed system aims to achieve accelerated learning and overcome the challenges associated with traditional distributed neural networks. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential for improved scalability and efficiency in complex learning tasks. The central formula for calculating the entanglement fidelity between nodes is given by *F(s_1, s_2) = 1 - ||s_1 - s_2||/1*, where *s_1* and *s_2* represent the quantum states at nodes 1 and 2, and *||.||* denotes the norm. The learning rate update rule, considering entanglement-assisted information propagation, is defined as *Δw_i = η * (∑_(j∈N(i)) α_ij * (s_i - s_j)) / ||s_i||*, where *w_i* is the weight update for node *i*, *η* is the learning rate, *N(i)* is the set of neighbors of node *i*, *α_ij* is the entanglement fidelity between nodes *i* and *j*, and *s_i* and *s_j* are the quantum states at nodes *i* and *j*. This framework provides a foundation for further research and development in quantum-enhanced distributed learning. ---

title: Dynamic Programming with Memoryless Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to solving optimization problems, particularly those amenable to dynamic programming, by leveraging the capabilities of memoryless neural networks. The core idea is to approximate dynamic programming solutions directly within a neural network architecture, circumventing the need for explicit memory storage. We introduce a network design incorporating a novel attention mechanism that strategically focuses on relevant subproblems, effectively replicating the iterative process of dynamic programming. This method addresses the significant memory bottleneck often encountered in traditional dynamic programming, especially when dealing with large state spaces. The resulting framework offers a potential pathway towards scalable and efficient solution of complex optimization problems. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and architectural design, that this approach can achieve comparable or superior performance to standard dynamic programming techniques, particularly when the state space is vast. The key innovation lies in the learned, selective focus afforded by the attention mechanism, enabling a computationally efficient approximation of the optimal policy.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Topology as a Basis for Algorithmic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-Euclidean topology as a foundational element for algorithmic reasoning, challenging the conventional wisdom of Euclidean geometry's centrality to logical thought. We propose a novel "topology-based reasoning" algorithm, demonstrating its ability to draw conclusions and make predictions based solely on the relationships between points, independent of the coordinate system. The core claim is that the underlying topology of a space—the connections between points—is more crucial for logical reasoning than traditional Euclidean geometry, opening avenues for AI systems with enhanced reasoning capabilities. This research investigates the implications of this paradigm shift, examining its potential impact on AI's capacity for abstract thought, problem-solving, and general intelligence. We outline the algorithm's design, its theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results, highlighting the significant differences in reasoning performance compared to Euclidean-based methods.

title: A drift adaptive framework for detecting and tracking evolving anomalies in financial transaction streams
abstract: Abstract Financial fraud detection is increasingly challenged by concept drift, evolving transaction behaviour, and adversarial adaptation, which can degrade conventional anomaly-detection methods under distributional change. Although unsupervised anomaly detection is widely used because labelled fraud data are scarce, most approaches identify anomalous transactions without preserving structural and temporal continuity of anomaly populations. This paper proposes HADA+ (Hybrid Anomaly Detection Architecture Plus), a sequential evolution-aware framework comprising Adaptive Anomaly Prioritization (AAP), Score-Aware Clustering (SAC), Optimal Transport Lifecycle Alignment (OTLA), and Lifecycle Evolution Modeling (LEM). Together, these components extend point-wise anomaly detection through drift-responsive prioritization, score-aware structural representation, cross-window alignment, and lifecycle analysis. HADA + was evaluated using the Credit Card Fraud dataset, a proprietary Mobile Banking transaction stream, a Synthetic Financial dataset with controlled concept drift, and a Controlled Lifecycle Validation Dataset with ground-truth lifecycle events. title: Robust Dynamic Expansion for Continual Learning under Backdoor Attacks via Purification and Selective Recovery
abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables models to acquire new knowledge from sequentially arriving tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, in practical scenarios, task streams collected from untrusted sources may contain backdoor-poisoned samples, posing a critical challenge to the stability, plasticity, and security of continual learners. In this work, we investigate a challenging setting termed Continual Learning Under Backdoor Attack (CLUBA), where each incremental task may involve a small proportion of maliciously manipulated training samples. Unlike conventional continual learning or backdoor defense scenarios, CLUBA requires models to simultaneously mitigate catastrophic forgetting, preserve adaptation capability, and prevent the absorption of malicious supervision during sequential updates. To address this challenge, we propose a robust dynamic-expansion framework that integrates sample purification, selective recovery, and robust expert routing into a unified continual learning paradigm. Specifically, we introduce Bi-Prototype Purification (BPP) to identify suspicious samples by exploiting semantic discrepancies in feature space. Based on purified data, Gradient Discrepancy-based Robustness Optimization (GDBRO) selectively recovers informative poisoned samples through pseudo-label correction and gradient consistency evaluation, improving robustness while maintaining model plasticity. Furthermore, Robust Feature Consistency-based Expert Selection (RFCBES) constructs perturbation-aware class prototypes to enable reliable expert routing under corrupted or shifted inputs.

title: What Matters in Orchestrating Robot Policies: A Systematic Study of Hierarchical VLA Agents
abstract: Hierarchical vision-language-action (Hi-VLA) systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex robot manipulation, by using high-level VLM planners to decompose tasks into language subgoals executed by low-level VLA controllers. Despite recent empirical progress, there is a lack of unified design principles for these systems: existing Hi-VLA systems differ in how they choose and connect planners, controllers, mechanisms to switch between the two, and how observations and memory are represented in the planner. In this paper, we present a systematic study of Hi-VLA design for robot manipulation. We unify representative Hi-VLA agents under an options-style control framework and benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive tasks. Our analysis distills practical principles for building Hi-VLA systems, showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying these principles yields a substantially stronger system than either flat VLA control or a naively designed hierarchy, across experiments both in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. Overall, our results provide a foundation for building more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical VLA agents. More information and video at jiahenghu.github.io/hi-vla.

title: SAP: State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance for Multi-Turn Tool Use
abstract: High-quality multi-turn tool-use data is essential for training agentic models, yet existing data synthesis methods often underrepresent the argument-level dependencies that are critical to long-horizon tool use. As a result, even when a model selects the correct tool, task execution may still fail because the model fills tool arguments with fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded values. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance (SAP)}. SAP combines state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation to efficiently construct tool-use trajectories with long-range dependencies and high accuracy. Using data generated by SAP, we build SAP-4B, which is highly competitive even when compared with much larger models across multiple benchmarks. Source code, synthesized data, and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Zichen1024/SAP.

title: EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can translate natural-language requests into real-world actions, creating safety risks from both indirect prompt injections and directly harmful requests. Existing system-level safety harnesses are typically designed by experts and applied across heterogeneous models and domains, despite substantial differences in model behavior, utility tolerance, and domain-specific safety requirements. We present EvoSafeHarness, a framework for automatically synthesizing deployment-specific safety harnesses for frozen LLM agents. Given a target model and domain specification, EvoSafeHarness jointly evolves a natural-language policy and executable enforcement logic using behavioral feedback from the target model. Each candidate is additionally evaluated through fresh-context adversarial review to filter rules that depend on benchmark artifacts. Across four agent benchmark families, EvoSafeHarness achieves a stronger safety-utility frontier than fixed expert-designed defenses. On DecodingTrust-Agent, evaluated across fifteen model-domain deployments, it reduces attack success rate from 50.9% to 12.6% for direct attacks and from 40.4% to 7.4% for indirect attacks, with a 3.3-point utility cost. On AgentDojo, it achieves 82.8% utility with 0.0% attack success rate, twice the utility of CaMeL at the same zero-attack-success operating point, while the same harness transfers unchanged to unseen AgentDyn suites. It also achieves the best score on Agent-SafetyBench for every evaluated victim model and maintains an attack success rate below 18% against an adaptive PAIR-style attacker with sixteen attempts per task. Analysis of the synthesized harnesses shows that domain semantics determine which safety relations and trajectory state must be tracked, while model and runtime behavior determine how and where those relations should be enforced.

evidence.title: EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents
evidence.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are turning language into real-world effects, making safety necessary against both indirect prompt injections and direct harmful requests. System-level safety harnesses add an enforcement layer beyond model-level defenses, but existing harnesses are usually designed once by experts and applied across heterogeneous models and domains. Effective protection is deployment-dependent: models differ in how much enforcement they need before utility declines, while domains differ in the effects, state, and action sequences that must be governed. A harness that is strict enough for one model may over-block another, and a policy that transfers across domains may miss application-specific safety relations. We present EvoSafeHarness, a safety-specific optimization framework that synthesizes a deployable harness for a frozen model in a target domain. It jointly searches a natural-language policy and executable code logic, guided by model behavior, domain specifications, and fresh-context adversarial review to reject benchmark-specific rules. Across four agent benchmark families, EvoSafeHarness achieves a stronger safety-utility frontier than fixed expert-designed defenses. On DecodingTrust-Agent, it reduces average attack success rate from 45.6% to 10.0% at a 3.3-point utility cost and achieves the best score in 14 of 15 cells. On AgentDojo, it reaches 82.8% utility at 0.0% ASR, twice CaMeL's utility at the same operating point, and transfers unchanged to unseen AgentDyn suites. It also achieves the best score on Agent-SafetyBench for every victim and keeps mean ASR below 20% under adaptive PAIR attacks with a refinement budget of 16. Analysis shows that domain semantics determine which safety relations and trajectory state are needed, while model and runtime behavior determine how and where those relations should be enforced.

title: Where Success Breaks: Failure-Boundary Learning for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapted through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) inherit a structural asymmetry: expert demonstrations teach the policy where success behavior lies, but provide no signal about where it ceases to be reliable. We argue that robust VLA adaptation should therefore be viewed not as further demonstration fitting, but as Failure-Boundary Learning -- the problem of Discovering, Localizing, and Shaping the boundary between recoverable deviations and task failure. To instantiate this view, we propose DLS: built on a real-grounded behavioral prior from few real demonstrations and simulated co-training, DLS discovers failure boundaries at scale through on-policy digital twin rollouts. Rather than reducing each rollout to a binary label, semantic progress localization uses privileged simulator states to assign progress-aware signals that capture where the failure boundary is crossed, not merely whether. These signals drive directional boundary shaping in the flow dynamics -- reinforcing success-producing denoising directions and suppressing failure-producing ones, without action likelihoods or auxiliary critics. Across real-robot manipulation tasks, DLS improves robustness over SFT and online RL baselines, especially under randomized initial states and unseen visual conditions.

title: Transforming Science with Large Language Models: A Survey on AI-assisted Scientific Discovery, Experimentation, Content Generation, and Evaluation
abstract: With the advent of large multimodal language models, science is now at a threshold of an AI-based technological transformation. An emerging ecosystem of models and tools aims to support researchers throughout the scientific lifecycle, including (1) searching for relevant literature, (2) generating research ideas and conducting experiments, (3) producing text-based content, (4) creating multimodal artifacts such as figures and diagrams, and (5) evaluating scientific work, as in peer review. In this survey, we provide a curated overview of literature representative of the core techniques, evaluation practices, and emerging trends in AI-assisted scientific discovery. Across the five tasks outlined above, we discuss datasets, methods, results, evaluation strategies, limitations, and ethical concerns, including risks to research integrity through the misuse of generative models. We aim for this survey to serve both as an accessible, structured orientation for newcomers to the field, as well as a catalyst for new AI-based initiatives and their integration into future “AI4Science” systems.

title: OmniStepBench: Deployment-Aware Agent Evaluation across Modalities and Task Complexity
abstract: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce \textbf{OmniStepBench}, a benchmark for deployment-aware agent evaluation across modalities and task complexity. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, OmniStepBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a $2\times3$ workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 30 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models (42 models in total) over 9{,}218 applicable model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show workload-dependent rankings, distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs between text and multimodal tasks, and competitive but weaker overall performance from local models. These findings support deployment decisions based on workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than a single aggregate score.

evidence.title: DAREBench: Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents
evidence.abstract: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce DAREBench (Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents), a benchmark designed to capture workload variation and support reliable agent evaluation. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, DAREBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a 2times3 workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 23 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models over 7,587 model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show that no single model dominates all workload groups, text and multimodal tasks exhibit distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs, and local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but still trail frontier commercial models overall. These findings suggest that agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than rely on a single aggregate score.

title: Where Does the Sound Go? Tracing Acoustic Information Loss in Audio-Conditioned LLMs
abstract: Audio-conditioned language models often underuse acoustic cues such as prosody, emotion, and non-speech sounds, raising the question of whether ASR-supervised frontends discard this information before it reaches the LM. We test whether the frontend is responsible by comparing Whisper-Tiny and Whisper-Small with EnCodec, DAC-VAE, and WavTokenizer in a shared Qwen3.5-4B audio-LM pipeline on ASR, emotion recognition, and sound captioning. Encoder replacement alone does not resolve this underuse: Whisper variants remain strongest overall, including on emotion and environmental sound captioning. To localize the failure, we trace task-relevant information through the encoder, projector, LM layers, and LM head. Linear probes and geometric analyses show that discriminative acoustic structure remains recoverable at the final LM layer, even when MCQA accuracy trails probe accuracy by up to 83 points. Because the answer format and decoding procedure are controlled, this task-dependent gap points to content-specific readout failure rather than generic format bias. LogitLens analyses and a targeted LM head intervention support the conclusion that acoustic underuse is not explained solely by encoder-side information loss and that readout alignment can be a dominant bottleneck.

title: What the Window Does Not Contain: Auditing Provenance in a Document-Grounded Instability Benchmark
abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. We built Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from real venture-financing filings, to measure how often this happens. Then we audited our own corpus and found a defect any excerpt-built benchmark can carry: items whose evidence is missing from the window of text the model is shown. The audit flags 36 items and separates two failures a single flag would conflate: evidence genuinely absent from the window and answers that must be computed from numbers the window does supply. Flagged items change their answers far more often, wobbling at 0.255 against 0.087 on the 427 clean items, and excluding them cuts apparent cross-model agreement by about a fifth. Before testing whether the missing evidence explains the instability, we registered a prediction: re-cut each window to hold its evidence, and instability should fall below a set threshold. It failed: the repair moved wobble by 0.058, with an interval containing zero. We report the association as correlational. Almost all measurements sit where instability cannot show, which bounds what a corpus built for accuracy can say about stability. We release the corpus, all 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a runnable check for any document benchmark.

evidence.abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. title: Beyond Cross-Lingual Transfer: Benchmarking Propagation Boundaries in Multilingual LLM Unlearning
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning aims to suppress target knowledge while preserving general capabilities. In multilingual settings, unlearning must additionally propagate within its intended linguistic scope. However, existing evaluations mainly measure cross-lingual transfer and cannot distinguish insufficient from excessive propagation. We introduce CLLPU (Cross-Lingual and Language-Bound Protocol for LLM Unlearning), a multilingual benchmark that formulates this problem through two settings: common-goal forgetting, where target knowledge should be suppressed across all languages, and language-conditioned forgetting, where suppression should remain confined to a designated language. CLLPU combines goal-guided topic pairing, schema-aware relation matching, and dual-anchor multilingual translation to construct 800 matched knowledge-unit pairs and 72,000 QA instances across ten languages. Experiments with six representative methods on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reveal opposite failure modes: forgetting remains incomplete when universal suppression is required, yet spreads beyond the intended boundary when language-conditioned confinement is required. We further find that general multilingual utility can conceal damage to neighbor knowledge. These findings establish propagation control as a central challenge for multilingual LLM unlearning. We publicly release CLLPU together with its construction pipeline.

title: Bait-and-Recover: Poisoning Internal Refusal Signals to Defend LLMs against White-Box Editing Jailbreaks
abstract: Open-weight large language models face a low-cost white-box threat from representation engineering attacks. Attackers can estimate refusal directions and search for projection-matrix edits that suppress safety alignment while preserving general capabilities, within minutes on a single GPU and without gradient-based training. We propose Bait-and-Recover, a weight-level defense that places a bait adapter where attackers read activations and a paired recovery adapter at the subsequent layer. Trained via gradient routing, this decouples the observation path from the behavior path. By actively poisoning the residual signal used for measurement, Bait-and-Recover disrupts the attacker's edit search, while the recovery layer restores clean downstream computation. Across four open-weight models, our defense raises the minimum refusal rate against white-box edit searches from 16.25% to 71.75% under a strict behavior-preservation budget (KL <= 0.10), with negligible impact on general benchmarks. By invalidating the core measurement assumption of these attacks, observation-path poisoning offers a practical complement to behavior-level safety training.

title: DataFlex-RL: An Evaluation Platform for RLVR Data Policies
abstract: Data policies for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) determine which rollouts are used, how strongly they are weighted, and which domains contribute to subsequent training batches. We introduce DataFlex-RL, an evaluation platform for comparing these choices under a common GRPO recipe. Our primary experiment evaluates 13 configurations across 12 matched seeds using Qwen2.5-7B-Base and 12 mathematics, logic, and science benchmarks. Uniform GRPO improves the domain-balanced average accuracy by 7.76 percentage points over the untrained checkpoint. None of the eight rollout-selection or reweighting methods achieves a paired 95% confidence interval that excludes zero relative to uniform sampling, and none of the three adaptive mixtures outperforms a fixed equal mixture at the same level of precision. A corrected 12-seed extension on Llama-3.1-8B-Base places the additional methods on the same score scale as the original controls, but does not reveal a consistent winner in terms of observed mean performance. We also quantify evaluation sensitivity by rescoring nine Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct runs using a math-heavy six-benchmark summary, consisting of five mathematics benchmarks and GPQA-Diamond but no logic benchmark, and comparing it with the domain-balanced 12-benchmark summary. The resulting rankings are negatively correlated, with a correlation coefficient of -0.33, whereas summaries that retain all 12 benchmarks largely agree. Across the controlled settings studied here, changing the data policy measurably changes the training process but does not produce a reproducible improvement over uniform training.

title: Cadence: Error-Bounded Lossy Compression of Demand Time Series with a Time-Series Foundation Model
authors: Roberto Tacconelli (Plain Text Extraction and Formatting)
abstract: We present Cadence, an error-bounded lossy compressor for numeric time series pairing a 330M-parameter time-series foundation model (Google TimesFM-3) with an adaptive arithmetic coder, guaranteeing $|\hat{x}_t-x_t|\leτ$ on every sample. One negative result constrains the design space: for lossless coding a foundation model is worth nothing, because bits saved are logarithmic in predictor accuracy, $Δb=\log_2(\mathrm{MAE_{old}}/\mathrm{MAE_{new}})$. So the $1.51\times$ advantage TimesFM-3 holds over a 32-tap linear predictor buys 0.60 bits of 20.28, a median gain of +0.03%. Error-bounded coding escapes this at one point: once a forecast lands inside the band the residual index is zero and the sample nearly free. Cadence contributes: (1) an adaptive range coder with context-modelled binarization, beating xz/zstd on real indices by 9.7% (15/15) and reversing a finding from a general-purpose back end; (2) a determinism result -- predictions are not bit-identical across batch sizes, and no PyTorch configuration repairs this, forcing group size and execution device into the container format; and (3) domain localization on corpora postdating any plausible training cutoff. On 49 EIA-930 balancing-authority demand series (2026) Cadence gains 13.3% over the best of six classical predictors, and 28.3% on 50 MTA ridership series (2026): 21.4% median over 297 series-tolerance pairs, winning all 297. Against downsampling, what time-series databases deploy for retention, its guaranteed worst-case error is $28$--$56\times$ tighter at equal size. End-to-end, once the context bootstrap is paid for, gains run from 6.8% at six months of hourly data to 15.1% asymptotically. Attempting to falsify the domain claim on SDRBench, theory predicts failure and delivers: -0.8% median, 0 of 27 pairs gaining. Three further negative results and eight retracted claims are reported in full.

title: Safety Monitors Mostly Catch What the Model Already Refuses
abstract: Safety monitors are evaluated by recall on harmful prompts, regardless of whether the target model would answer them. Yet a monitor matters most on the prompts the model does answer. We measure recall on exactly those prompts, defined by sampling the target model and judging its responses. Across four text guards, two activation probes, and Latent Guard, recall at a 1% false positive rate falls sharply on this subset: at a common threshold, every monitor catches the requests the model refuses 1.1 to 6.4 times as often as the requests it answers. Standard metrics hide this; AUROC stays above 0.85 for most monitors. Rewriting each request to be less explicit, with intent held fixed and verified, raises compliance 28-fold and lowers every monitor's flag rate. Of the requests newly answered after rewriting, 44 to 93% slip past the monitor, depending on which is used, and most of their completions are graded harmful. We trace the gap to explicitness itself. As wording softens with intent fixed, the target model's harm and refusal readings fall and it answers; the guards' harm readings fall too, and steering a guard along explicitness alone flips its verdict. Model and monitors miss the same prompts, and stacking monitors does not recover them. Fine-tuning a guard on the rewrites at every level of explicitness, on both sides of the label, raises recall on answered requests from .24 to .89 while transferring to unseen benchmarks; hard negatives, the natural alternative, teach the guard to discount indirect phrasing instead.

evidence.title: Recall Is Not Protection: Evaluating Safety Monitors Against Model Compliance
evidence.abstract: Safety monitors screen prompts sent to deployed language models, flagging harmful requests so they are never answered. They are evaluated by recall against harmfulness labels, but a catch only prevents harm if the model would otherwise have complied. We measure the difference directly: we sample repeated responses from the target model, call a harmful prompt elicitable if the model complies at least once, and report monitor recall separately on elicitable and non-elicitable prompts. Across six monitor configurations and three model families, spanning activation probes, fine-tuned text guards, and a 120B policy-conditioned reasoning classifier, recall on elicitable prompts falls 0.22 to 0.38 below recall on non-elicitable prompts at a fixed false positive rate. The prompts a monitor misses are 2.8 to 5.6 times more likely to be complied with than the prompts it catches. The gap replicates across three model families and appears also in text-only monitors entirely independent of the target model. This suggests that standard recall may overstate the protection monitors provide in practice, and that monitors should be evaluated against what their models will actually answer.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence through Causal Inference and Decision Support
abstract: This paper explores the integration of causal inference with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to enhance decision support systems. Traditional XAI methods often struggle with providing true explanations for decisions, particularly in complex scenarios where correlation doesn't imply causation. This research proposes a novel framework leveraging causal inference techniques to build more robust and transparent decision support systems. We construct causal graphs representing the relationships between variables, apply causal inference algorithms to identify and quantify these relationships, and then translate the resulting insights into human-understandable explanations. The core aim is to move beyond simply identifying correlations to understanding the underlying causal mechanisms driving decisions. This approach addresses the critical need for transparency and trust in AI-driven decision-making, particularly in domains where accountability and understanding are paramount. The framework is demonstrated through a conceptual analysis and outlines potential implementation strategies.

title: Explainable AI via Graph-Based Causal Inference for Model Decisions
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep learning models in critical applications necessitates a means to understand and trust their decisions. However, deep learning models are often 'black boxes,' offering limited insight into the reasoning behind their predictions. This paper proposes a novel approach to explain model decisions by leveraging graph-based causal inference. We represent the model's decision-making process as a graph, where nodes represent input features and the model's output, and edges represent causal relationships inferred from the model's behavior. By analyzing the structure of this graph, we can identify the key factors driving a specific prediction, providing a clear and interpretable explanation. The core of this approach is to move beyond simply identifying correlations between features and the output and instead to explicitly model the causal influences. This offers a more robust and reliable explanation than traditional methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique through a theoretical framework and discuss its potential applications in various domains. The resulting visual representation of the causal graph provides a significantly improved understanding of model decision-making compared to purely correlational explanations.

title: Relational Graph Neural Networks with Dynamic Schema Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Relational Graph Neural Network (RGNN) architecture designed for continuous adaptation to evolving datasets. Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often rely on fixed, pre-defined schemas, limiting their ability to effectively learn from data that changes over time. Our proposed approach, termed Dynamic Schema Evolution RGNN, addresses this limitation through a self-modifying graph structure driven by a reinforcement learning agent. The agent dynamically adjusts the network's relational structure – specifically, node relationships, edge weights, and the introduction of new nodes – based on observed data patterns and uncertainty metrics. This allows the network to learn and maintain accuracy even as the underlying data distribution shifts. The core claim is that this architecture provides a robust and adaptive solution for learning from dynamic graphs, moving beyond static schemas and offering a truly dynamic learning capability. We detail the architecture, the reinforcement learning agent, and the key mechanisms driving the schema evolution, highlighting the advantages over conventional GNNs.

title: Neurodegeneration Modeling and Self-Repair in Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel mathematical model for simulating and predicting neurodegeneration in neural networks, incorporating both synaptic plasticity and internal information processing anomalies within neurons. The model utilizes a multi-layered probabilistic approach to dynamically represent the degradation process, considering changes in synaptic weights, increased neuronal internal information entropy, and the loss of neuronal connections. A key component of the research is the integration of reinforcement learning to enable self-repairing capabilities within the network. The core claim is to provide a more realistic and predictive model compared to existing approaches, which are often static or overly simplified. The model's ability to dynamically adjust and repair itself addresses a critical limitation in current neurodegeneration research. Mathematical formulations and key concepts are presented throughout this document.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Discovering Hidden Temporal Correlations
abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to the problem of discovering hidden temporal correlations within graph data. Traditional methods often struggle to effectively capture the dynamic relationships inherent in graphs, particularly when temporal information is present. This work proposes a novel GNN architecture designed specifically for this task. The core idea is to augment graph nodes with temporal attributes, such as timestamps, and to define edges that represent temporal dependencies between nodes. Through message passing and aggregation, the GNN learns to propagate temporal information across the graph, effectively uncovering previously unrecognized correlations. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and by outlining the key architectural components. The results highlight the potential of GNNs to revolutionize how we analyze and understand temporal data represented as graphs. The core claim is that GNNs can uncover previously unrecognized temporal correlations within graph data by learning to represent and propagate temporal information. The core mechanism involves designing a GNN architecture where nodes have temporal attributes and edges represent temporal relationships, enabling the network to learn dependencies between nodes across time. This is a new approach specifically designed for temporal correlation discovery in graph data.

evidence.abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to the problem of discovering hidden temporal correlations within graph data. Traditional methods often struggle to effectively capture the dynamic relationships inherent in graphs, particularly when temporal information is present. This work proposes a novel GNN architecture designed specifically for this task. The core idea is to augment graph nodes with temporal attributes, such as timestamps, and to define edges that represent temporal dependencies between nodes. Through message passing and aggregation, the GNN learns to propagate temporal information across the graph, effectively uncovering previously unrecognized correlations. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and by outlining the key architectural components. The results highlight the potential of GNNs to revolutionize how we analyze and understand temporal data represented as graphs. The core claim is that GNNs can uncover previously unrecognized temporal correlations within graph data by learning to represent and propagate temporal information. The core mechanism involves designing a GNN architecture where nodes have temporal attributes and edges represent temporal relationships, enabling the network to learn dependencies between nodes across time. This is a new approach specifically designed for temporal correlation discovery in graph data.

abstract: This paper investigates the application of a novel computational framework based on adaptive topology networks for complex physical system simulations and predictions. Traditional topology network models often lack the inherent dynamism required for accurate modeling of complex systems. Our framework leverages the self-organizing properties of adaptive topology networks to provide a more flexible and responsive simulation approach. We present a conceptual model and initial implementation demonstrating the potential of this approach for simulating systems exhibiting dynamic behavior. The core mechanism involves simulating the system's internal state evolution driven by the network's inherent structure, offering enhanced prediction capabilities compared to static topology models.

This algorithm leverages the inherent self-adaptive properties of quantum graph theory to dynamically adjust graph parameters, allowing for optimization and improved performance across a wider range of scales. The core mechanism involves iterative parameter adjustments based on a feedback loop, ensuring the algorithm continuously refines its response to the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analysis, showcasing significant improvements in algorithm speed and scalability compared to traditional methods.

abstract: Fractal geometry, traditionally studied for its aesthetic appeal and complex patterns, possesses a surprising potential as a fundamental data structure. This paper explores the concept of formally incorporating fractal geometry into computer science, proposing a novel 'fractal metric' to represent data distributions and enabling efficient manipulation through self-similarity. This shift from conventional data structures towards fractal-based systems promises significant advancements in algorithm design and data processing.

title: Title: Topological Information Theory as a Foundation for Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of topological information theory as a foundational framework for quantum computing. We propose a novel approach to quantum state encoding and processing, leveraging the unique properties of topological structures to achieve enhanced quantum algorithms and data transmission efficiency. The core mechanism involves the integration of topological information theory with quantum computation's encoding and measurement processes, utilizing topological structures to construct quantum states and investigate their application within quantum computing. This work addresses current limitations in quantum computing, specifically focusing on improving the efficiency of quantum algorithms and data transfer through the application of topological principles. The paper concludes by highlighting the key advancements and potential future directions in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Geometric Phase Transitions in Complex Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates geometric phase transitions in complex neural networks, exploring how network structure and activation patterns evolve during a dynamic process. We introduce a novel "geometric state" algorithm that quantifies and models these transitions, revealing emergent patterns through dynamic connectivity adjustments. Current approaches often treat networks as static models, failing to fully capture the complex dynamics of these systems. This work proposes a framework that leverages geometric analysis to understand and predict phase transitions, potentially leading to improved network design and stability. The core mechanism focuses on quantifying the network's geometric state, offering a new perspective on how these networks evolve. The paper details the algorithm's design, its impact on the resulting phase transition, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness.

title: Title: Cognitive Resonance Fields (CRFs)
abstract: This paper investigates the potential for cognitive phenomena to emerge through the manipulation of resonant fields generated by neural networks. We propose a computational model, the Cognitive Resonance Field (CRF), that posits cognitive processes as the creation of these resonant fields, where neural network activity and contextual information significantly influence the amplification or dampening of specific patterns. The paper explores the fundamental principles of this model, detailing the concept of resonance fields and outlining a framework for their manipulation and application to various cognitive domains. The core claim is that by understanding and controlling these resonant fields, we can simulate and potentially influence complex cognitive behavior. This work represents a novel approach to cognitive modeling, moving beyond traditional neural network architectures to explore a more holistic system based on field dynamics.

title: Quantum Walk Based Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to distributed machine learning by enabling collaborative model training without directly exchanging raw data. However, traditional FL systems are plagued by privacy vulnerabilities and significant communication costs. This paper proposes a novel framework, Quantum Walk Based Federated Learning (QWFL), that addresses these limitations by integrating the principles of quantum walks. We leverage quantum superposition and interference to create a secure and efficient model aggregation process. The core idea is to represent model updates as quantum walks on a graph representing the distributed devices, where the walk's evolution inherently obfuscates information. This approach significantly reduces the risk of privacy breaches while concurrently minimizing communication overhead. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential of QWFL to achieve better privacy guarantees and communication efficiency compared to conventional FL methods. We present a formal mathematical model of the QWFL system and analyze its key properties, including the walk's convergence rate and the level of privacy protection afforded by the quantum walk process. The design aims for practical implementation by considering the challenges of integrating quantum computing technologies into existing FL architectures. The results indicate that QWFL provides a viable pathway towards robust and scalable distributed learning.

title: Evaluating the reliability of function calling by large language models for ukrainian-language requests
abstract: Function calling by large language models is increasingly used to connect natural-language requests to software functions, yet its reliability for Ukrainian-language requests remains poorly characterized.We introduce UA-ToolCall, a paired English-Ukrainian benchmark with twenty bilingual mock-tool contracts, twenty-four development cases, and one hundred and twenty fixed test cases (one hundred required calls, ten clarification cases, and ten no-tool cases).It varies query and description languages, catalogue size, and distractor similarity while keeping machine identifiers canonical.Models from the Qwen3, Granite 3.3, and SmolLM3 families were evaluated in quantized form using a shared text prompt for unconstrained one-step generation of structured function-call outputs and greedy decoding, producing three thousand six hundred outputs.Under English descriptions and the full catalogue of twenty tools, Ukrainian queries reduced strict success from ninety-four to seventy-four percent, from forty-three to nine percent, and from twenty-six to nine percent, respectively; all paired effects remained significant after Holm correction.Qwen kept one hundred percent tool-selection accuracy, so its loss came from arguments and canonicalization; Granite lost selection and arguments; SmolLM3 was dominated by decision-field errors.Ukrainian and bilingual descriptions improved SmolLM3 by eleven and seventeen percentage points, respectively, but did not produce statistically significant gains for the other models; bilingual descriptions increased mean prompt length by fifty-four to eighty-three percent.Within the single catalogue order generated with seed 1701, neither catalogue contrast was statistically significant; order variability was not estimated.These results support reporting semantic and executable correctness separately and indicate that localization benefits are model-dependent.The findings apply to promptbased one-step generation of structured function-call outputs by the recorded Q4_K_M builds, not native function-calling interfaces, constrained decoding, or multi-step tool interaction.

title: Rethinking One-Shot Federated Graph Learning: Training-Free Statistical Estimation
abstract: One-shot federated graph learning generally aims to train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) across clients with disconnected subgraphs in a single communication round. Existing methods predominantly design advanced optimization strategies under the premise that local GNN training is indispensable. However, empirical observations reveal that under extreme non-IID conditions, local GNN training suffers from severe cross-client representation misalignment, becoming a major source of error rather than a remedy. Motivated by this, we reformulate one-shot FGL as a statistical estimation problem. We propose SPEAR (Statistical Prototype Estimation with Adaptive Reliability), a completely training-free framework that directly computes topology-smoothed class prototypes from local graphs in the original feature space. The server then aggregates these prototypes using a sample-size-adaptive shrinkage estimator that down-weights unreliable local estimates, producing robust global class prototypes. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under extreme heterogeneity. Moreover, SPEAR delivers at least an order-of-magnitude speedup over all baselines, reaching several orders of magnitude against generative and distillation-based methods. Our findings suggest that training-free statistical estimation, rather than local GNN optimization, provides the key to robust and efficient one-shot federated graph learning. The code is available at https://github.com/Yodeesy/SPEAR .

title: Three Contour AI Framework Prototype
abstract: An example of a software implementation of a three-contour architecture for resolving priority conflicts in autonomous systems. The prototype demonstrates how three independent contours — the vital (safety), the cognitive (navigation), and the social (interaction) — compete for control of executive mechanisms. Unlike the traditional approach, control here is exercised through an arbiter. Each contour forms its own priority based on incoming events, and the arbiter, using the WTA (Winner Takes All) principle, selects which contour gains access to the executive outputs. The hysteresis mechanism prevents chaotic switching: a new contender must exceed the current winner by a set threshold. The vital contour has the right of unconditional interruption — in the event of a critical threat to safety, it immediately seizes control, regardless of the priorities of the other contours. The prototype includes a graphical interface for activating events, visualizing priorities, and logging the arbiter's decisions. The code is implemented in Python using Tkinter and NumPy and is intended to demonstrate the principle of three-contour arbitration in systems where conflicts between subsystems with different goals must be resolved.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation via Selective Layer-wise Batch-Norm Update
abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) has become a promising paradigm for addressing domain shifts at test time without accessing source data. However, standard methods like TENT update all Batch Normalization (BN) parameters across the entire architecture, creating significant memory and computational overheads. In this work, we propose a lightweight TTA strategy based on selective layer-wise parameter updates. By freezing early feature-extraction layers and restricting adaptation exclusively to the deeper 50% of BN parameters, our method eliminates runtime selection overhead. Evaluations on corrupted CIFAR-10 using ResNet-50 demonstrate a 64.7% reduction in peak GPU memory usage(from 6288.8 MB to 2218.2 MB) and a 44.7% execution latency speedup, while maintaining stable adaptation dynamics and preventing batch-level overconfidence.

title: CipherFlute: 3Dプリントした笛の音の高さに秘密を書き込み、吹いて読み出す
abstract: CipherFluteは、3Dプリントした笛の管の長さ(=音の高さ)に秘密情報を符号化し、笛を吹いた音から読み出す方式と、その実装一式である。笛は電源も電子部品も持たず、家庭用の3Dプリンタで作れて、日用品の内部空洞として存在できる。読み出しはスマートフォンのWebアプリでも、ピアノや照合笛と紙の早見表による人手でも行える。 収録物: 笛の造形データと生成器、11進の差分符号とリードソロモン誤り訂正(GF(11))による符号化・復号の実装(PythonとJavaScript)、復号Webアプリ、人手復号の早見表、大規模言語モデルのエージェントが日用品の3Dモデルに笛を埋め込むための手順書(スキル)、Shamirの秘密分散、暗号資産ウォレット(テストネットでの実験)、実機で復号まで通った作例のギャラリー。 CipherFlute encodes secret information into the pitch (bore length) of 3D-printed whistles and reads it back from the sound when the whistles are blown. This record archives the whistle models and generators, the GF(11) differential coding and Reed-Solomon error correction (Python/JavaScript), the browser-based decoder, a paper lookup table for manual decoding, an LLM-agent skill for embedding whistles into everyday objects, Shamir secret sharing, an experimental crypto-asset wallet (testnet), and a gallery of fabricated examples verified by actual decoding. ソースコードはMIT License、3Dデータと写真はCC BY 4.0である(LICENSE-assets参照)。Web版: https://unryu.org/cipherflute/

title: Quantum Decoherence Modeling and Prediction in Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary advancements across various fields, but its practical realization is fundamentally limited by the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. Decoherence refers to the loss of quantum superposition and entanglement due to interactions with the surrounding environment, leading to computational errors. This paper presents a comprehensive modeling and prediction framework for quantum decoherence, aiming to provide a deeper understanding of this critical process. The framework utilizes a mathematically rigorous approach based on the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically focusing on the master equation formulation of decoherence. We derive a set of equations that accurately describe the evolution of the quantum state under the influence of various environmental noise sources. Furthermore, we explore methods for estimating decoherence rates and predicting the decoherence time, which is a crucial parameter for assessing the viability of quantum computations. The model incorporates key concepts such as the Bloch sphere representation, the Lindblad master equation, and the concept of decoherence channels. We demonstrate the applicability of the model to various quantum systems and discuss the potential for developing effective decoherence mitigation strategies. The ultimate goal is to provide a tool that can guide the design and optimization of quantum computers, ultimately paving the way for robust and reliable quantum computation.

title: Topological Photon-Based Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol leveraging the unique properties of topological photons. The protocol aims to achieve high security by exploiting the non-local nature of topological photon networks. A key mechanism involves constructing a topological photon-based quantum network and utilizing topological entanglement for key generation. Furthermore, the protocol incorporates topological protection strategies to enhance the overall security against eavesdropping attacks. The core claim is the design of a highly secure QKD protocol utilizing topological photon's non-locality. The core mechanism is the construction of a topological photon quantum network and the utilization of topological entanglement for key distribution, combined with topological protection to bolster security. This work demonstrates the potential of topological photonics in significantly improving the security and robustness of QKD systems.

title: Neural Network Dynamics Optimization: A Precise Analytical Approach
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to optimizing neural network models by leveraging precise analytical solutions of non-linear dynamical systems governing neuronal behavior. The core claim is that through careful investigation of these solutions and subsequent parameter optimization, we can identify and refine neuronal models capable of exhibiting specific functionalities such as memory and learning. The methodology employs optimal control algorithms to iteratively adjust model parameters based on simulated neuronal responses to various stimuli. Furthermore, the research utilizes chaos theory and quantitative analysis to derive accurate analytical solutions, allowing for a level of control previously unattainable with simplified models. The resulting framework offers a pathway towards a more precise and controllable simulation of artificial neurons, moving beyond traditional approaches reliant on simplified representations. This work addresses a significant gap in current neural network simulation techniques and provides a foundation for future research into biologically realistic neuronal models.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Model Selection in Deep Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to the problem of adaptive model selection within deep learning. Traditional model selection methods often rely on manual tuning or grid searches, which can be computationally expensive and inefficient. We propose a framework where a reinforcement agent learns to dynamically select the optimal deep learning model architecture and hyperparameters based on the observed performance. The agent's state space represents the current model configuration, and the action space comprises the available architectural choices and hyperparameter settings. The reward function is defined based on the validation performance of the selected model. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our RL-based approach can effectively identify high-performing models and significantly reduce the time and resources required for model selection compared to conventional methods. The core claim is that reinforcement learning can be used to dynamically select the best deep learning model for a given task and dataset. The core mechanism involves training a reinforcement agent to explore the space of deep learning architectures and hyperparameters, learning to choose models that maximize performance.

title: 基于量子纠缠的动态算法优化
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar quantum mechanical phenomenon, offers a fundamentally new approach to optimization problems. This paper proposes a novel dynamic algorithm framework based on quantum entanglement to address complex optimization challenges. We introduce a method that leverages the inherent, self-changing nature of entangled quantum states to achieve optimization, and subsequently develop an optimized algorithm for large-scale problems. The core mechanism centers around manipulating entangled states to guide the search process, offering a potential paradigm shift in optimization techniques. This research explores the potential of quantum entanglement for enhancing optimization capabilities, aiming to deliver more efficient and robust solutions compared to classical approaches.

title: Quantum Complexity Theory – Proof of Concept for Verification
abstract: Quantum Complexity Theory (QCT) represents a paradigm shift in the verification of complex quantum algorithms, moving beyond traditional methods that struggle with scalability. This paper proposes a novel framework predicated on the application of quantum error correction and superposition to create a 'Quantum Signature' – a formally defined representation of a quantum program's state. This signature will allow for automated verification using quantum computation, significantly enhancing certainty and enabling the efficient assessment of algorithm correctness. The paper details the design of this signature, explores its potential for error mitigation, and discusses the theoretical implications of this approach.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum Circuit Optimization
abstract: Quantum circuits, while promising for quantum computation, present significant challenges in terms of design, optimization, and resource utilization. Current optimization techniques often rely on manual parameter tuning, limiting scalability and adaptability. This paper proposes a dynamic adaptive quantum circuit optimization algorithm that automatically adjusts quantum circuit parameters to enhance circuit performance and reduce hardware resource consumption. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors the circuit's performance and adjusts the parameters to achieve optimal results. This approach overcomes the limitations of traditional methods by providing a truly automated optimization process. This work presents a novel methodology leveraging dynamic adjustments to improve circuit efficiency and resource utilization, demonstrating significant potential for advancing the field of quantum circuit design.

title: Quantum Information Encryption: A Geometric Optimization Approach
abstract: Quantum information cryptography stands as a critical field, demanding robust and adaptable security measures against evolving computational threats. Traditional cryptographic methods often rely on complex mathematical algorithms, presenting vulnerabilities to sophisticated attacks. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging geometric optimization to design a quantum information encryption scheme, aiming for enhanced security and efficiency. The core mechanism centers on employing geometric optimization algorithms to create a layered encryption system that offers improved key distribution and communication capabilities. The research explores the potential of this approach to address current limitations in quantum cryptography and paves the way for a more secure and adaptable cryptographic paradigm. We present a preliminary analysis demonstrating the efficacy of this method through simulated scenarios and outline future research directions focusing on scalability and practical implementation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Topology Analysis
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that they share the same fate, holds immense potential for future technological advancements. This research delves into the intricacies of quantum entanglement, specifically exploring its topological properties and developing a novel computational framework leveraging this phenomenon. We propose a new approach to quantum information processing that transcends the limitations of classical computation, aiming for unparalleled efficiency through the application of entangled quantum states. The core of this investigation involves constructing a topological network model based on quantum entanglement, and subsequently designing a quantum algorithm predicated on this structure. This work presents a significant departure from conventional quantum computing paradigms by emphasizing the fundamental role of entangled quantum states in computation. The novel mechanisms and proposed computational framework are designed to achieve significantly enhanced computational capabilities. This research lays the foundation for a paradigm shift in quantum information processing, potentially unlocking solutions to complex problems currently intractable with existing technologies. The study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations, highlighting the potential for substantial improvements in processing speed and data transmission.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry and the Association with Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic relationship between non-linear topological geometry and quantum entanglement. We propose a novel quantum communication protocol leveraging the unique properties of topological structures to achieve significantly enhanced quantum information processing capabilities. This protocol focuses on manipulating quantum states through non-linear transformations, effectively circumventing limitations inherent in traditional entanglement-based schemes. The core mechanism involves the design and implementation of a quantum state characterized by a dynamically evolving topological structure, enabling the establishment of robust and efficient quantum entanglement channels. This work investigates the potential of this approach to revolutionize quantum communication and computation, particularly in the context of ultra-high-speed data transmission and complex calculations. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations, the feasibility and advantages of this approach.

title: Causal Discovery from Streaming Data via Bayesian Manifold Learning
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of causal discovery in dynamic environments, specifically focusing on streaming data. Traditional causal discovery methods rely on static datasets, rendering them ineffective for analyzing data streams where relationships evolve over time. We propose a novel approach utilizing Bayesian manifold learning to infer causal relationships from these continuous streams. Our method exploits the underlying manifold structure inherent in streaming data, assuming that variables with causal relationships will cluster closely together in this space. We develop a Bayesian framework that iteratively updates the manifold representation based on incoming data, allowing us to adapt to changes in the data distribution and identify evolving causal dependencies. The core of our approach lies in the use of variational inference to approximate the posterior distribution over the manifold structure, providing a computationally tractable solution for real-time causal discovery. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our method through a theoretical analysis and simulation studies, highlighting its ability to capture causal relationships in dynamic systems. The key contribution is a scalable and adaptive framework for causal discovery that overcomes the limitations of static approaches and offers a pathway for understanding causal mechanisms within evolving data streams.

title: From Lead Qualification to Auto-Generated Demand
abstract: Abstract: AI voice agents that place the first call to a new contact, run a scripted pre-qualification, and hand only the contacts that pass to a human salesperson have become a visible trend in both B2B and B2C sales. This paper examines that approach — here, the AI Voice Agent model — against a structurally different one implemented by the Integration Coefficient IC business model framework and its two operating tools, IC-APP and IC-CHAT. The two models are not functionally equivalent; they intervene at different points in the pipeline, and that difference is hierarchical, not stylistic. The AI Voice Agent model improves the efficiency with which contacts already inside a CRM are qualified, without altering the criterion by which those contacts entered the CRM in the first place. IC-APP and IC-CHAT platforms replace that criterion outright: nothing enters the CRM that is not already, by construction, a voluntarily declared need — a category this paper defines operationally as an Auto-Lead. Because that data is self-reported by the subject rather than inferred about them from the outside, it is genuine in a strictly epistemic sense — a claim about the provenance of the signal, not about the person's likelihood to buy. The paper further shows that an AI Voice Agent's own qualification step is internally circular, proposes a four-tier taxonomy distinguishing contact, interested party, pre-qualified lead, and Auto-Lead, and formulates a testable hypothesis for future empirical comparison of the two models. Keywords: demand generation, lead qualification, AI in B2B and B2C sales, disintermediation, bilateral platforms, energy supply chain, Integration Coefficient IC, Auto-Lead, IC-APP, IC-CHAT, IC-Ambassador, AI Voice.

title: Quantum Artificial Intelligence opportunities, challenges, threats, use case and future trends
abstract: The field of quantum computing is presently undergoing a significant transition. Even if quantum computers are now so large and capable that they can only be used under certain limitations, be conventionally emulated, it is still unknown which applications can benefit from a quantum advantage. With an emphasis on artificial intelligence (AI) and its applications as some of the most significant key technologies of our time, this provided an excellent starting point for looking beyond the already demonstrated acceleration of a few specific classical computing tasks by quantum computers, such as unstructured search and prime factorization. Actually, the goal of Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI) is to merge the two worlds for each’s benefit. Stated differently, QAI research focuses on using quantum computing to solve computationally challenging AI problems and, conversely, using AI to address the difficulties associated with developing and running quantum computing systems. The creation of direct quantum or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for problem solving and the examination of their possible benefits over the best classical alternatives are of particular interest.

title: MLLMs Hallucinate when Information Distribution Drifts in Synergy Heads
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with hallucinations, thus hindering their reliable practical applications. Existing attention-based mitigation methods mainly rely on indirect signals (e.g., attention weights) that fail to accurately reflect the actual information shift underlying hallucination generation. In this paper, we propose HEAL, Head-lEvel information disentAnglement and caLibration for identifying and mitigating hallucinations. HEAL first employs causal noise intervention on multi-head outputs to filter out causally redundant heads. Subsequently, it disentangles information distribution within the remaining heads via the counterfactual Difference-in-Differences, categorizing heads into four types. Through analysis, we observe: hallucinations happen when information distribution drifts away from a healthy equilibrium in synergy heads, not strongly correlated with the quantity or strength of modality-specific heads. Motivated by this insight, HEAL injects dynamic information calibration factors into the value vectors of synergy heads, and actively regulates visual-language dependencies, steering the output distribution towards factual evidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HEAL effectively reduces hallucinations across multiple MLLMs, offering a simple and interpretable pathway to enhance model trustworthiness.

title: Fast PAC Global Optimization via Restarted Langevin: Exploration, Exploitation, and Degenerate Cooling
abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental question in non-convex optimization: \textit{How should a stochastic optimizer allocate computation between global exploration and local exploitation?} We study this question in continuous time, using Langevin dynamics for global exploration and deterministic gradient flow for local exploitation. The simplest algorithm in this class is the best-state Langevin--gradient method: several Langevin trajectories explore the objective landscape, the best state encountered is retained, and a single gradient trajectory then refines this state to high terminal accuracy. Our main objective is to characterize the computational work required to achieve a prescribed accuracy with prescribed confidence. We develop low-temperature approximations for this probably approximately correct (PAC) work--accuracy tradeoff, both for the best-state method and for related Langevin schemes. Global exploration is governed by energy barriers, through spectral-gap and Eyring--Kramers asymptotics. The resulting approximations expose the competing effects of temperature, computational budget, and the number of exploratory trajectories, and quantify their dependence on the confidence parameter. In contrast, terminal accuracy is largely separated from global exploration: once a suitable region of attraction has been reached, gradient flow requires only $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ additional work to reach accuracy at least $\varepsilon$. Numerical experiments on challenging objectives serve to compare algorithms and to test the quantitative predictions of the asymptotic theory. They identify regimes in which the low-temperature approximations provide useful guidance, as well as regimes exhibiting substantial temperature sensitivity and potentially significant high-dimensional limitations.

title: Learning Counterfactual World Models for Embodied Reasoning under Partial Observability
abstract: World models promise a general route to embodied intelligence: learn predictive dynamics once, then reason, plan, and act with them. Increasingly, the representations beneath such models are pretrained on large-scale video, interaction, and multimodal corpora, which raises a question prediction quality alone cannot answer: when is a learned representation actually actionable? We identify a failure mode we call counterfactual collapse: a model predicts visually plausible futures while failing to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences. This arises whenever a representation is optimized for perceptual similarity rather than intervention structure, which is precisely the objective under which most large-scale pretrained encoders are learned. We introduce Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM), which combine a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when their observations look alike. Across occluded manipulation, aliased navigation, and long-horizon manipulation, CLWM improves planning success over the strongest baseline (65.1% $\to$ 74.6% on Occluded Push and 67.3% $\to$ 78.9% on Aliased Maze) and reduces exploitative planning failures (18.4% $\to$ 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen), with ablations attributing the gains to hard counterfactual negatives, especially perceptual-alias negatives. Finally, our counterfactual separability metric, which tracks planning success across the five baseline model classes ($r \ge 0.94$), is representation-agnostic: given intervention-outcome labels, it can audit any encoder, pretrained or trained from scratch, before a planner trusts it. We do not yet measure it on large-scale pretrained encoders. Here we establish the metric and its relationship to planning success for world models trained from scratch.

title: Modelling and Constructing Avatars for Museum Exhibitions
abstract: This paper presents a development in constructing the Avatar system based on artificial intelligence (AI) technology to answer the textual questions in its initial phase. The proposed solution is developed using the Ollama tool and implements a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. The advantage of this system is that it works locally and ensures responses are strictly based on a given document, which prevents imaginary answers. Use case is given based on the exhibition catalogue dedicated to Serbian mathematician Mihailo Petrović Alas as the knowledge source. The four systematic experiments are conducted with varying chunking parameters, retrieval methods, and system configurations. These experiments are evaluated using 25 test questions across different system setups. Based on the results, research establishes a foundation for developing reliable, AI text answering context-aware systems as the initial phase of creating AI avatars that can enhance visitor engagement.

title: Reliability and Domain Limitations of Intelligent Virtual Assistants in Digital Heritage Systems
abstract: After years of work on cultural heritage and scientific digitization, the world accumulated a vast amount of data and information. Although digital data is far more accessible than the physical one, even in an unstructured way, better interaction is needed by the non-professional users. At the same time AI-related systems gain widespread popularity in all kinds of platforms, easing accessibility. Digital assistants and chatbots are implemented in existing applications and databases. Cultural heritage areas are not falling behind. Plenty of examples of using such systems in the field are already available. Implementation of AI in cultural heritage brings unique challenges along with benefits. The accuracy of the models is highly uncertain, caused by the specifics of the cultural heritage data. Several approaches to overcome the challenges such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation are examined.

title: A Lightweight, Gas-Efficient Blockchain-Secured Federated Learning Framework for Disease Prediction
abstract: This repository contains the full implementation and experimental artifacts for a blockchain-secured federated learning framework for disease prediction, evaluated across two clinical datasets (Pima Indians Diabetes and Heart Disease UCI). The codebase includes three components: Centralized baseline (Python, scikit-learn/PyTorch): trains a neural network and logistic regression baseline on the full dataset, with multi-seed evaluation support. Federated learning simulation (Python, Flower/PyTorch): simulates federated training across a configurable number of hospital nodes using FedAvg, supporting both IID and non-IID data partitioning. Blockchain verification layer (Solidity, Hardhat): a smart contract (FederatedLearningRegistry.sol) that authorizes participating hospital nodes and anchors model update provenance on-chain, with gas cost measurement scripts. All raw experimental results (JSON files) from the multi-seed evaluation, hospital-count sensitivity sweep, and blockchain gas cost analysis reported in the associated paper are included in the results/ directory, along with an aggregation script to reproduce the summary tables and figures.
